questions.enonce_markdown: Explain why metabolic reactions occur in small steps. *[5 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Metabolism is organised into **pathways** (e.g. glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, the Calvin cycle) in which a large change is split into **many small steps**, each catalysed by its **own specific enzyme**. The advantages are:

1. **Energy is released gradually in small amounts** that cells can capture in **ATP** (about 40 % in aerobic respiration). If the energy of glucose were released in one step, most of it would be lost as **heat** and could **damage the cell** and denature its proteins.
2. **Every step can be controlled separately:** an enzyme can be switched on or off by its product (**feedback inhibition**), by inhibitors, activators or by changes in pH, so the cell regulates the rate of the whole pathway and does not waste materials.
3. **The reactions can take place at body temperature and neutral pH:** enzymes lower the activation energy of each small step, so no violent conditions are needed.
4. **Intermediate compounds can be used for other pathways** (e.g. intermediates of the Krebs cycle are used to make amino acids and fats), and the pathway can be **branched or reversed**.
5. **The product of one step is the substrate of the next**, so the enzymes can be arranged in sequence (on membranes or in multi-enzyme complexes), which makes the pathway **fast and efficient**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Describe and illustrate how the following factors affect the rate of enzyme reaction.

(i) Substrate concentration.

(ii) Temperature and temperature coefficient.

(iii) Hydrogen ion concentration. *[12 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Substrate concentration** (enzyme concentration, temperature and pH kept constant).

- At **low substrate concentration** the rate rises **in direct proportion** to the concentration: many active sites are free, so more **enzyme-substrate complexes** form as collisions become more frequent.
- As the concentration increases, the active sites fill up and the rate rises **more slowly**.
- At **high concentration** all the active sites are occupied (the enzyme is **saturated**) and the rate **levels off at the maximum rate, $V_{max}$**. Adding more substrate has no effect; only **more enzyme** would increase the rate. The substrate concentration that gives half of $V_{max}$ is the **Michaelis constant $K_m$** (a low $K_m$ means a high affinity of the enzyme for its substrate).

*Graph:* rate of reaction (vertical axis) against substrate concentration (horizontal axis): a curve starting at the origin, rising steeply, then bending over to a **horizontal plateau at $V_{max}$**.

**(ii) Temperature and temperature coefficient.**

- From low temperatures up to the **optimum** (about 37 $^\circ$C for human enzymes, 40 to 50 $^\circ$C for many plant and microbial enzymes), the rate **rises** because the molecules gain **kinetic energy**, collide more often and with more energy, so more enzyme-substrate complexes form.
- The **temperature coefficient, $Q_{10}$**, is the **factor by which the rate increases for a 10 $^\circ$C rise in temperature**: $Q_{10} = \dfrac{\text{rate at } (T+10)\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}}{\text{rate at } T\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}}$. For enzyme-controlled reactions $Q_{10} \approx 2$ below the optimum (the rate **doubles** for every 10 $^\circ$C). This applies **only below the optimum**: above it the rate falls and $Q_{10}$ is less than 1.
- Above the optimum, the increasing vibration **breaks the hydrogen and ionic bonds** that hold the **tertiary structure**, so the **active site changes shape** and the enzyme is **denatured (irreversibly)**; the rate falls rapidly to zero (at about 60 to 70 $^\circ$C for most enzymes). At low temperature (near 0 $^\circ$C) the enzyme is only **inactive**, not denatured, and works again on warming.

*Graph:* rate against temperature: a curve rising slowly, then steeply, to a **peak at the optimum temperature**, followed by a **sharp fall** (an asymmetrical bell shape).

**(iii) Hydrogen ion concentration (pH).**

- Each enzyme has an **optimum pH** (pepsin about 2, salivary amylase about 6.8 to 7, trypsin about 8) where the rate is **maximum**.
- A change in H$^+$ concentration alters the **ionisation (charge) of the R groups** of the amino acids, especially those in the **active site**. This disturbs the **ionic and hydrogen bonds** that keep the tertiary structure, so the active site no longer fits the substrate (and the charge of the substrate may change too): the rate **decreases on both sides of the optimum**.
- **Extreme pH values denature** the enzyme permanently.

*Graph:* rate against pH: a **symmetrical bell-shaped curve** with the peak at the optimum pH (for pepsin the peak is at an acid pH, for trypsin at an alkaline pH).

questions.enonce_markdown: Differentiate between competitive and non-competitive inhibitors. *[3 marks]* *(5, 12, 3 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
| Feature | Competitive inhibitor | Non-competitive inhibitor |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | **Similar in shape to the substrate** | **Not similar** to the substrate |
| Binding site | Binds to the **active site** and competes with the substrate | Binds to **another site** (the allosteric site), away from the active site |
| Effect on the enzyme | Blocks the active site | **Changes the shape of the active site**, so the substrate cannot fit |
| Effect of more substrate | The inhibition is **reduced or overcome** when the substrate concentration is increased | **Not overcome** by increasing the substrate concentration |
| Effect on $V_{max}$ and $K_m$ | $V_{max}$ unchanged; $K_m$ increased (apparent) | $V_{max}$ **decreased**; $K_m$ unchanged |
| Example | Malonate on succinate dehydrogenase (substrate: succinate) | Cyanide on cytochrome oxidase; heavy metal ions such as Hg$^{2+}$ and Ag$^+$ |

Both are usually **reversible** (except some poisons that bind permanently).
